title: Building Context-Aware Reasoning Applications with LangChain and LangSmith: Harrison Chase
talk_summary: Harrison Chase lays out a taxonomy of context sources (instructions, few-shot, retrieval, fine-tuning) and reasoning architectures (single call, chain, router, while-loop agent, autonomous agent), arguing you should pick the simplest architecture that fits. He then names the real engineering pain points: orchestration choice, data engineering for context, prompt debugging, evaluation (lack of data and metrics), and collaboration.

takeaways.technique: Match architecture to task; prefer chains/routers over autonomous loops
takeaways.what_they_do: They classify reasoning apps on a spectrum from fixed chains (known steps, more control) to routers (LLM picks a branch) to while-loop agents to fully autonomous agents, and argue none is superior — chains give control, agents handle unexpected inputs.
takeaways.evidence_quote: chains are really good because you have more control over the sequence of steps that are taken agents are better because they can more dynamically react to unexpected inputs

takeaways.what_they_do: Use a cheap LLM call to decide which prompt, which model, or which tool to invoke based on the input, rather than hardcoding one path.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can use it to route between uh language models so one model might be better than another

takeaways.technique: Build eval datasets from production traffic + LLM-assisted grading
takeaways.what_they_do: Because zero-shot models let you ship without a dataset, they recommend harvesting real traffic and hand-labeled or LLM-generated examples into an eval set, and using LLM-assisted evaluation plus tracked feedback as the practical metrics.
takeaways.evidence_quote: those can come from either labeling data points by hand or looking at production traffic and pulling things in

takeaways.technique: Inspect the fully-formatted prompt at each step
takeaways.what_they_do: They stress that debugging means seeing exactly what the model receives after system instructions, few-shot examples, retrieved context, chat history, and prior agent steps are combined — hard once the app has run several steps.
takeaways.evidence_quote: what does this all look by the time it gets to the language model

takeaways.technique: Few-shot for tone/structured output; fine-tune only at scale
takeaways.what_they_do: They map context types to use cases: instructions for behavior, few-shot when behavior is hard to describe (tone, structured output), retrieval for grounding, fine-tuning when you need thousands of examples of a fixed format.
takeaways.evidence_quote: structured output is a good use case for this you can give examples of the of the structured output format

takeaways.what_they_do: They note the most common agent loop breaks work into discrete states — plan, execute, validate — often validating with a separate LLM call, versus asking one autonomous agent to do all implicitly.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the most common one that we see are kind of like plan execute and validate
